title: Composing layers
goals: Trace how one layer supplies the next layer inputs
Check that connected layer dimensions and feature order agree
Explain why intermediate activations are not automatically class predictions

prerequisite.prompt: For z = -2 and z = 3, what does ReLU return? Does this operation itself assign a class?
prerequisite.answer: ReLU returns 0 and 3. It transforms a numerical score. A class prediction requires a separate declared output rule.

vocabulary: A group of computations that maps an input vector to an output vector
An intermediate value computed inside a network
Applying one function to the output of another
Computing successive values from an input using fixed parameters

lesson.title: Connect computations with an explicit contract

blocks.text: A network connects layers so that the output vector of one layer becomes the input vector of the next. Use a fictional numerical input x = [x1, x2]. The first layer computes z1 = x1 - x2 and z2 = x1 + x2 - 2, then applies ReLU separately: h1 = max(0, z1), h2 = max(0, z2). Its output is the ordered vector h = [h1, h2].

The next layer computes y = 2h1 - h2 + 1. It receives h, not the original x. It uses weights [2, -1] and bias 1, with identity as its output activation. This is a two-layer computation when counting the layers with weights; an input placeholder is not counted here. All parameters are supplied, so this lesson performs no training.
The two first-layer units both receive the same original x. They can be calculated in either order. Only after both activations are available do we evaluate the output layer.

Take x = [3, 1]. First compute z1 = 3 - 1 = 2 and z2 = 3 + 1 - 2 = 2. ReLU gives h = [2, 2]. The output layer receives exactly this ordered pair and returns y = 2 times 2 - 2 + 1 = 3. Record z, h and y separately so that a correct final number cannot hide an incorrect intermediate step.

blocks.title: Optional Python check
blocks.text:
def forward(x):
    if len(x) != 2:
        raise ValueError("Expected two input components")
    x1, x2 = x
    z = [x1 - x2, x1 + x2 - 2]
    h = [max(0, value) for value in z]
    y = 2 * h[0] - h[1] + 1
    return z, h, y

print(forward([3, 1]))  # ([2, 2], [2, 2], 3)
print(forward([1, 3]))  # ([-2, 2], [0, 2], -1)

The code assumes numeric inputs with the agreed meaning. Its length check does not validate units or field order. Python indices 0 and 1 correspond to the first and second hidden components. There is no feedback from y into h during this forward calculation.

blocks.title: Complete each stage before using its output
blocks.caption: Read the rows from top to bottom. The first two rows together form the hidden layer; the final row is the output layer. Each row shows the values actually passed to the next stage.

blocks.label: Trace x = [1, 1]. Record z1, z2, h1, h2 and y. Explain why using x directly in the output formula would be a different model.

blocks.text: The output layer expects two inputs because its two weights match h1 and h2. If the hidden layer is redesigned to return three activations, the output layer needs a compatible three-input definition. Silently dropping an activation or inventing a third weight does not preserve the stated model.

Order matters even when lengths match. For x = [4, 1], h = [3, 3] happens to be unchanged by swapping, so that case cannot reveal an order bug. For x = [3, 0], h = [3, 1] gives y = 6. Swapping only those hidden values gives 2 times 1 - 3 + 1 = 0. Swapping both the values and their matching weights would preserve the dot product.

Keeping the output layer fixed, replacing ReLU with identity changes the model. For x = [1, 3], identity gives h = [-2, 2] and y = -5; ReLU gives h = [0, 2] and y = -1. More layers or a different activation do not establish better predictions without valid evaluation.

The computed y is a numerical output, not a verified probability or a class by itself. If we separately declare class 1 when y >= 0 and class 0 otherwise, the worked inputs [3, 1] and [1, 3] receive classes 1 and 0. Their true labels are not supplied, so these calculations do not measure accuracy.

A hidden value is a computed feature. We should not name h1 as confidence or h2 as danger without evidence for that interpretation. Distinct inputs may also produce the same hidden vector: [0, 1] and [0, 2] both give h = [0, 0] and y = 1. A later deterministic layer seeing only h cannot recover the lost distinction.

blocks.label: A team says its output is correct because all layers connect and its code runs. Which claim has it checked, and what evidence is still missing?

blocks.text: Next week uses longer forward-pass tables to locate the first incorrect intermediate value and check complete network calculations.

workbook.title: Trace the second worked case
workbook.prompt: For x = [1, 3], write both scores, both ReLU activations and y using the lesson model.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Scores are -2 and 2; activations are 0 and 2; y = 0 - 2 + 1 = -1.

workbook.title: Repair a dimension mismatch
workbook.prompt: A revised hidden layer returns [h1, h2, h3]. The output layer still has weights [2, -1]. Explain the mismatch and what must be specified before calculation.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Three hidden values need three matching weights under this dense output definition. Specify all three coefficients and the bias or explicitly design a documented selection operation. Do not silently drop the third value.

workbook.title: Use a revealing order check
workbook.prompt: Compare hidden vectors for x = [4, 1] and x = [3, 0]. Which input reveals a bug that swaps h1 and h2 but keeps output weights unchanged? Give correct and swapped outputs for that input.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: The first gives [3, 3] and cannot expose a swap. The second gives [3, 1]; correct output 6 becomes 0 when values alone are swapped.

workbook.title: Compose a new network independently
workbook.prompt: A new model takes [u, v]. Compute a = ReLU(u + v - 3), b = ReLU(u - v), then q = a + 2b - 1. Trace both inputs [2, 1] and [1, 2], including scores before ReLU. Apply class 1 when q >= 0. State the hidden and output vector sizes.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: For [2, 1], scores 0 and 1 give [a, b] = [0, 1], q = 1 and class 1. For [1, 2], scores 0 and -1 give [0, 0], q = -1 and class 0. Hidden dimension is 2; output dimension is 1. The equality at hidden score zero produces activation zero, not an automatic final class.

workbook.title: Explain information loss
workbook.prompt: Use the lesson model to verify h and y for [0, 1] and [0, 2]. Could a fixed later layer receiving only h distinguish the two original inputs?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Scores are [-1, -1] and [-2, 0]. Both produce h = [0, 0] and y = 1. A deterministic later computation given the same h produces the same result; additional original-input information would require a changed architecture.

teacher.background: Teach composition through explicit numerical traces in two 45-minute sessions. Keep the layer definition, order and activation visible. The aim is to understand which values each computation receives, not to memorise a network drawing or claim successful training.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook; paper and pencil
Calculator and optional local Python 3 editor; no packages or AI accounts needed
Use the fictional examples supplied; prepare the fresh retry before class
sessions: Retrieve ReLU at negative, zero and positive scores. Ask students to distinguish an activation from a class.
Write both first-layer formulas side by side. Draw arrows from the same x to both; label the ordered hidden output.
Trace [3, 1] together, then use W1. Require scores before ReLU and output contributions after ReLU.
Run or trace the optional Python and complete the guided [1, 1] case. Ask why directly substituting x into the output formula is incorrect.
Retrieve the two layer input/output sizes. Let students describe composition in one sentence.
Complete W2 and W3. Compare a swap-insensitive case with a revealing case before discussing bug coverage.
Collect W4 independently before hints. Check both pre-activation scores, both activations, q and class under the declared threshold.
Complete W5 and the exit response. Give targeted feedback and the fresh retry without replacing the original assessment record.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: x = [1, 1] gives z = [0, 0], h = [0, 0], y = 1. Using x directly would give 2, skipping the hidden transformation. Exit: compatible shapes and execution check whether the specified computation can run, not whether predictions match real labels. Accuracy requires appropriate labelled examples, a metric and independent evaluation.
misconceptions: The second hidden unit receives the first hidden unit output
Both units in this hidden layer receive x. The next layer receives the pair of activations after both are computed.
Two numbers mean the connection must be correct
Matching lengths do not establish matching order or meaning. Trace a case with unequal hidden activations.
A hidden unit is already a class prediction
Its activation is an intermediate numerical feature. A declared output rule assigns the final class.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires both complete traces, correct classes and sizes. Fresh retry: a = ReLU(u - 1), b = ReLU(v - 2), q = 2a - b. Inputs [0, 3] and [2, 2] give pre-activation scores [-1, 1] and [1, 0], hidden vectors [0, 1] and [1, 0], and q values -1 and 2. Under q >= 0 their classes are 0 and 1. Ask which vector the output layer actually receives.
teacher.support: Provide a five-column trace table labelled x, z, h, output contributions and y. Allow arithmetic support while requiring the student to name each connection. Extension: replace hidden ReLU with identity and simplify the lesson network to y = x1 - 3x2 + 3. Test [1, 3] to show that the simplified affine model differs from the ReLU model.
